answers.children: Ibizan Hounds are moderately good with children when raised together. Their athletic build, independent nature and high prey drive mean they can become overly excited around small children during play, and their history of hunting in packs on the Balearic Islands gives them a chase instinct that requires supervision with little ones. The breed bonds subtly rather than with constant affection.
answers.other-pets: Ibizan Hounds do not reliably get along with other pets. Their high prey drive, bred for hunting rabbits and small game over rocky terrain, makes them likely to chase cats and other small animals, while their aloof temperament can lead to tension with unfamiliar dogs.
answers.exercise: Ibizan Hounds need at least an hour of vigorous daily exercise. Bred for speed, agility and leaping across rough Balearic terrain while hunting, they become restless and prone to destructive digging or fence scaling without running, lure coursing or long hikes that stretch their lean athletic build.
answers.shedding: Yes — Ibizan Hounds shed moderately with short smooth coats that produce visible hair on furniture and clothing year round. The single-coat texture lacks the heavy undercoat of double-coated breeds so the hair is fine and short yet still requires regular removal to prevent accumulation in the home, and their low-maintenance coat aligns with the breed's overall easy-care profile from its utilitarian peasant origins.
answers.hypoallergenic: The Ibizan Hound has a short smooth coat that sheds lightly and produces minimal loose hair around the house. This low-maintenance single coat requires only occasional wiping to stay clean, fitting the breed's athletic build developed for hunting rabbits over rocky Balearic terrain. No breed is genuinely hypoallergenic yet the Ibizan Hound is not among those usually suggested to allergy sufferers.
answers.training: Ibizan Hounds are not easy to train. Their independent streak and intelligence, forged by centuries of hunting rabbits without constant human direction on the Balearic Islands, make them stubborn and less biddable than breeds developed for close partnership, so they respond best to patient, challenge-based methods that respect their athletic mind.
answers.lifespan: Ibizan Hounds live 11-14 years. Their hardy build and health robustness developed through peasant farming on rugged Spanish islands support a relatively long life for a medium sighthound, with the lean athletic frame and low-maintenance coat contributing to overall vitality when given appropriate exercise.
answers.size: Ibizan Hounds reach 45-65 lb and stand 22-27 in tall. Their elegant long-legged proportions and lean athletic build feel lightweight and graceful to live with, allowing bursts of exceptional speed while the medium size suits a dog that can leap and turn nimbly yet still fit comfortably in a vehicle or home.
answers.barking: Ibizan Hounds do not bark a lot. Bred as quiet hunters that rely on sight and speed rather than voice while pursuing game in packs across the Balearic Islands, they remain reserved and almost cat-like indoors, saving their voice for genuine excitement or alarm and staying generally silent compared with more vocal hounds.
answers.apartment: Ibizan Hounds can live in an apartment only with exceptional daily exercise. Their high energy, athletic leaps and independent nature mean they settle quietly indoors once exercised but become destructive or restless without at least an hour of running, and their aloof watchdog tendencies add minimal noise once the prey drive is satisfied.
answers.first-time: Ibizan Hounds are not a good first dog. Their independent intelligence, high prey drive and need for structured athletic outlets demand an experienced owner who can manage the aloof temperament and stubborn recall failures that stem from their history of self-reliant hunting on rocky Spanish terrain.
